notes.meaning: A new message begins. The bright vision of God's glory had left Ezekiel, but God's word still came to him. God can keep speaking to his people even without visions or special experiences.

God reminds Ezekiel that the people around him are a "rebellious house." They can see and hear, but they refuse to. Their blindness comes from their stubborn hearts, not from any lack of ability. God says this so Ezekiel won't lose heart when people pay no attention.

differ.view: People are not lost because God's grace was not enough. They are lost because they misused the grace they were given.

notes.meaning: Ezekiel is told to pack an exile's bag, the kind of thing a person carries when forced to live far from home: a staff, a bag, food and clothes. Then he is to move from his place in full view of everyone. He was already an exile in Babylon. Now he acts it out to warn that the people still in Jerusalem would soon follow. "Perhaps they will understand" teaches that God's servants should keep going even when they see little result.

During the day Ezekiel carries his bags out where people can see them. In the evening he leaves himself, the way captives are led away. This pictured King Zedekiah's escape by night when Jerusalem fell. Matthew Henry adds a lesson: hold this world loosely, because we have no lasting city here.

Ezekiel does not go out the door. He digs through the wall, like someone who knows the door is guarded and has to slip away in secret. This pointed to the way Zedekiah and his men would escape through a gap in Jerusalem's wall.

He carries his load on his shoulder in the dark, with his face covered, like a person afraid of being recognized and too ashamed or sad to look around. Adam Clarke also sees a hint that Zedekiah would be blinded. God calls Ezekiel a "sign," a warning picture of what was coming. As Ezekiel did, so the people would do.

Ezekiel did exactly as he was told, even though he knew people would laugh at him. He cared more about pleasing God than about being mocked. His example teaches us to obey God gladly, even when it is hard.

differ.view: Ezekiel really did these things in public, and the morning message in verse 8 shows the act had taken place.

notes.meaning: The explanation did not come until the next morning, which kept Ezekiel relying on God. The people had asked, "What are you doing?" God calls them "rebellious" again because they were not asking sincerely. They were making fun of him.
A "burden" is a heavy message of coming trouble. The "prince" is King Zedekiah, the very ruler the exiles were trusting to rescue them. He and all the people in Jerusalem would share this fate.

"I am a sign to you" means that what Ezekiel acted out would really happen to the people of Jerusalem. They would be taken away as captives. It also ended the exiles' hope of a quick return home. As Wesley puts it, we cannot assume the place we live is the place we will rest.

The king himself would sneak out in the dark, carrying his own things, through a hole in the wall, with his face hidden. This came true when Zedekiah fled Jerusalem by night (2 Kings 25:4; Jeremiah 39:4). As Matthew Henry says, God's judgments can turn a prince into a porter.

The Babylonian army was God's net. The king could not slip out of it. He would be taken to Babylon and die there, yet never see it, because his eyes were put out at Riblah. Jeremiah said he would see the king of Babylon. Both prophets were proved right.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think a prediction this exact must have been written after Jerusalem fell. The Pulpit Commentary mentions this view and rejects it.

notes.meaning: The king's bodyguard and his troops would be scattered in every direction, with the sword chasing after them. The Babylonians did the fighting, but God says he is the one doing it. Even unbelieving nations are in his hands.

When the people are scattered among the nations, they will finally know that God is the LORD. They had laughed off his warnings. Now they would learn the hard way, through his judgment. Calvin urges us to know God early, by faith, while there is still time.

God would spare a few from war, hunger and disease. In foreign lands they would tell of their own sins. Then the nations would see that God let his people fall because he was punishing sin, not because he was weak. Matthew Henry sees God bringing good out of evil: scattered sinners become scattered penitents (people who are sorry for their sin) who honour God in other lands. Calvin thought their sad condition itself told the story of their sins.

A second sign: Ezekiel must eat and drink while shaking with fear. It pictured how frightened people in Jerusalem would be during the siege, unable to enjoy a meal in peace. Ezekiel was not pretending. He truly felt the sorrow of what was coming. Matthew Henry says those who warn others of judgment should speak with real feeling.

The exiles envied those still in Jerusalem, but Jerusalem's people were really worse off. The worst was still ahead of them. Their land would be stripped bare and their cities left empty. The cause was the violence and injustice they did to one another. Through it they would come to know the LORD.

A saying had spread among the people: "Time goes on, and the prophecies never come true." Because judgment had not come yet, they decided it never would. God's patience was meant to lead them to repent, which means to turn from their sin. Instead they used it as an excuse to keep sinning. Compare the scoffers in 2 Peter 3:3-4.
God will put a stop to their saying. They said every vision fails. God says the days are near when every vision will come true. Far from being delayed, the judgment was already at the door.

The false prophets who promised peace, and their "divination" (trying to read the future by tricks), would be shown up by what actually happened. When God speaks, it comes to pass, because his word and his action never pull apart. "In your days" means the very people who mocked would live to see it.

A second group did not call Ezekiel a liar. They simply said his warnings were about the far-off future, so they did not need to worry. Matthew Henry notes that people often treat death and judgment this way, as if they were far away, when they may be very near.

God's answer is firm: no more delay. What he has said will be done. He had waited in order to be gracious, but they abused his mercy. No one can push away the evil day except by seeking peace with the Lord.
